topic.subject: science
topic.title: Structure of the atom
topic.scope: electrons, protons, neutrons, Thomson and Rutherford models, Bohr model, valency, atomic number, isotopes

misconceptions.statement: Atoms are solid spheres like tiny marbles with no internal parts.
misconceptions.why: Students often struggle to visualize entities that are too small to be seen and rely on macroscopic analogies.
misconceptions.fix: Atoms are mostly empty space containing a dense nucleus surrounded by moving electrons.

probe.question: What is inside a single atom of gold?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a solid piece of gold matter all the way through.

misconceptions.statement: Electrons are just tiny dots of matter that stay fixed in place.
misconceptions.why: Textbook diagrams often show static positions for electrons, ignoring their constant motion.
misconceptions.fix: Electrons are particles that move rapidly in specific regions around the nucleus.

probe.question: Do electrons ever stop moving inside an atom?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they stop moving once they find a stable spot.

concepts.name: Evolution of Atomic Models (Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr)

misconceptions.statement: Rutherford's model proves that electrons orbit the nucleus exactly like planets orbit the sun.
misconceptions.why: The 'planetary model' analogy is frequently used in classrooms to simplify Bohr's theory.
misconceptions.fix: While electrons move around the nucleus, they do not follow simple, fixed circular paths like planets.

probe.question: Why don't electrons fall into the nucleus if they are orbiting?
probe.wrong_answer: They are held in orbit by gravity just like planets.

concepts.name: Atomic Number, Mass Number, and Isotopes

misconceptions.statement: Isotopes of an element have different chemical properties because they have different masses.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse physical properties (mass) with chemical properties (reactivity).
misconceptions.fix: Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they behave identically in chemical reactions.

probe.question: Will Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 react differently with oxygen?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because Carbon-14 is heavier, it will react slower.

misconceptions.statement: Valency is simply the number of electrons in the outermost shell.
misconceptions.why: Students often fail to distinguish between valence electrons and the combining capacity (valency).
misconceptions.fix: Valency is the number of electrons an atom needs to gain, lose, or share to complete its octet.

probe.question: What is the valency of Chlorine (atomic number 17)?
probe.wrong_answer: 7, because it has 7 electrons in its outer shell.
